stem: A client has taken a proton-pump inhibitor (PPI) long term but no longer has a clear ongoing indication. Which deprescribing teaching is most accurate?

options.A: Use an exact eight-week taper for every long-term PPI user because any faster reduction causes permanent pathologic acid hypersecretion.
options.B: Explain that transient rebound upper-GI symptoms may occur after long-term PPI discontinuation and that either dose tapering or abrupt discontinuation can be considered.
options.C: Never stop a PPI abruptly because rebound symptoms are uniformly dangerous and cannot be managed clinically.
options.D: Continue the PPI indefinitely after the original indication has resolved because long-term duration alone creates a maintenance indication.

rationale: AGA Best Practice Advice states that patients who discontinue long-term PPI therapy should be advised that transient upper-GI symptoms may occur from rebound acid hypersecretion and that either dose tapering or abrupt discontinuation can be considered. Patients without a definitive chronic indication should be considered for a trial of deprescribing. B is correct.
educational_objective: Teach clients that transient rebound symptoms can occur when long-term PPIs are stopped and that either tapering or abrupt discontinuation may be considered when deprescribing is appropriate.
source_document_title: De-prescribing proton pump inhibitors (PPIs) — Clinical Practice Update

source_locator: Best Practice Advice 2, 8, and 9: patients without a definitive chronic indication should be considered for deprescribing; warn of transient upper-GI symptoms due to rebound acid hypersecretion; either dose tapering or abrupt discontinuation can be considered.
source_claim_supported: When long-term PPI therapy no longer has a clear indication, deprescribing may be considered; clients should be warned about transient rebound symptoms, and tapering or abrupt discontinuation are both acceptable approaches.

source_original.stem: A client has taken a proton-pump inhibitor (PPI) long term but no longer has a clear ongoing indication. Which deprescribing teaching is most accurate?

options.A: Require an exact eight-week taper for every long-term PPI user because any faster reduction produces permanent pathologic acid hypersecretion.
options.B: Warn that transient rebound upper-GI symptoms may occur after long-term PPI discontinuation and that either tapering or abrupt stopping can be considered.
options.C: Avoid abrupt discontinuation in every patient because rebound symptoms are uniformly dangerous and cannot be managed clinically.
options.D: Continue the PPI indefinitely after one year of treatment even when the original indication has resolved and no maintenance indication remains.

source_original.rationale: AGA best-practice advice supports regular review of indication, warns about transient symptoms from rebound acid hypersecretion after long-term discontinuation, and states that dose tapering or abrupt discontinuation can be considered.
source_original.source_detail: Best Practice Advice 8–10. AGA Clinical Practice Update on PPI de-prescribing; live guidance currentness rechecked 2026-08-15. NCSBN first-check: Overview of Content — Pharmacological and Parenteral Therapies, printed p.12: medication administration, controlled substances, adverse effects/interactions, monitoring and teaching. 2026 NCLEX-RN Test Plan; effective 2026-04-01 through 2029-03-31; currentness rechecked 2026-08-15.

correction_summary: Retained the deprescribing construct and key B, corrected the exact AGA locator to include Advice 2/8/9, removed overstatements about fixed taper duration and dangerous rebound, and reduced difficulty from hard to medium.

audit_findings.source_authority: AGA Clinical Practice Update; NCSBN 2026 Test Plan
audit_findings.claim_audit: Final item accurately conveys rebound-symptom counseling and acceptable discontinuation approaches when deprescribing is indicated.

distractor_audit.A: Incorrect; AGA does not require a universal fixed taper.
distractor_audit.B: Correct and directly supported by Best Practice Advice 8 and 9.
distractor_audit.C: Incorrect; abrupt discontinuation can be considered.
distractor_audit.D: Incorrect; lack of ongoing indication supports considering deprescribing rather than indefinite continuation.

audit_findings.ambiguity_second_answer: Only B matches AGA guidance without adding unsupported absolutes.
audit_findings.cueing: All options are deprescribing teaching statements of comparable structure.
audit_findings.blueprint: Pharmacological and Parenteral Therapies — medication management and teaching.
audit_findings.independent_second_pass: Re-read the AGA Best Practice Advice list, all options, rationale, objective, ambiguity and blueprint mapping. B remained uniquely correct.
